newsitem.title: HAITI: Haitian leader faces chorus of criticism.
newsitem.headline: Haitian leader faces chorus of criticism.

text.p: Haiti's President Rene Preval, trying to put the poorest nation in the Western Hemisphere back on its feet, is entering the New Year facing a chorus of criticism and calls to step aside.

In an effort to quell the anger, Preval threw an early New Year's celebration at the presidential palace on Monday and gave an optimistic speech -- but the sight of government leaders downing champagne at 10:30 a.m. was unlikely to bolster popular support.
Parliamentarians and popular leaders over the weekend called Preval's government incompetent and ineffectual.

"This has been a catastrophe," Serge Gilles, leader of the centrist Nationalist Progressive Party for the Haitian Revolution, said in radio broadcasts. "This government has been characterised by insecurity and economic decline."

Among those calling for the government to step aside were former Port-au-Prince Mayor Evans Paul, leader of the National Front for Change and Democracy, and Mirlande Manigat, former senate candidate and wife of former President Leslie Manigat.

The Preval administration, whose February inauguration marked the first transfer of power between two democratically elected governments in Haiti, was not given much to work with. It inherited a budget deficit as large as the budget and an inexperienced police force incapable of maintaining order.

Haiti is mending from a 1991 coup and three years of brutal military rule in which an estimated 5,000 people were killed. Jean-Bertrand Aristide, Haiti's first freely elected president, was restored to power by U.S. troops in 1994.

U.N. peacekeepers continue to patrol Haiti's streets. Last month their mandate was extended for the third time, until the end of July, because the fledgling police force is not ready to maintain national security.
In recents months Haiti has been plagued by a rising crime rate and strikes by government employees, including hospital and sanitation workers, who have not been paid in months.
In a television interviewed aired on Sunday, Aristide criticised Preval's government and its economic policies, but stopped short of calling for the administration to step aside.
"There is increasing desperation," Aristide said, citing a 75 percent unemployment rate that he said could increase under a privatisation plan championed by Preval and Prime Minister Rosny Smarth.

The plan, approved by Parliament, would privatise nine state-run enterprises through joint ventures or concession and management agreements. While privatisation will bring hundreds of millions of dollars in U.S. aid and private investment, there has been mounting popular opposition to the idea.
"Right now we heavily depend on the international community," Preval said. "We need the money for our budget."
At least 60 percent of the $893 million budget now being debated in Parliament would be funded by the international donors, through loans and grants. The 1995-96 budget was only $130 million.
While the wave of New Year's criticism seemed to have sent a message to government leaders, Preval told Reuters it did not mean disaster for his administration.
"It is easy for people to criticise when they aren't the ones doing the work to solve the problems," he said. "But this is a democracy, and people can say what they want."
